title: Why cursor pagination beats huge offsets
subtitle: Make large result sets more predictable
learning_objective: Choose offset or cursor pagination based on dataset size and consistency needs.

scenes.title: PAGE 500 IS SLOW
scenes.body: Your API fetches page 500 by skipping thousands of rows before returning 20 results.

scenes.title: Offset asks the database to skip
scenes.body: Offset pagination is simple, but large offsets can require increasing work. Inserts or deletes between requests can also shift page boundaries.

scenes.title: Stable ordering matters
scenes.code:
SELECT id, created_at
FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) > ($1, $2)
ORDER BY created_at, id
LIMIT 20;

scenes.title: Avoid skipped or repeated rows
scenes.body: Use a deterministic ordering with a unique tie-breaker. Cursor design must match the database and the intended consistency behavior.

scenes.question: Why include a unique tie-breaker in cursor ordering?
options: To make ordering deterministic when timestamps tie
To eliminate the need for an index in every case
scenes.explanation: Rows with the same primary sort value need a stable secondary key so pagination can continue without ambiguity.

scenes.title: Remember this
scenes.body: Offset is convenient for small lists; cursor pagination often scales better for large, changing feeds.
